title: Open the Garden Gate
description: Check that your Java tools are ready without trying to learn everything at once.
instructions: Open a terminal and run java --version.
Open the editor you plan to use for the course.
Create a folder where your small Java programs can live.
Write down one setup question if anything is unclear.
evidenceChecks: I saw a Java version in the terminal.
I know where I will save my Java files.
hints: This is only a readiness check. You do not need to configure every editor feature.
If the terminal cannot find Java, note the exact message for a tutor or the course setup guide.
The course expects a JDK, not only a JRE. The JDK includes tools used to compile programs.
It is completely valid to finish this task as stuck and bring the saved error to Tutor Corner.

questions.prompt: Which Java toolset includes the javac compiler needed to compile source files?
questions.correctExplanation: Correct. The Java Development Kit (JDK) includes javac and the tools needed to develop Java programs.
questions.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The compiler is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK), not a browser or a runtime-only installation.

mascotMessage: A clear setup question is progress too.

title: Wake Up a Tiny Program
description: Type, compile, and run a small Java program yourself.
instructions: Create a file named HelloGarden.java.
Type a class named HelloGarden with a public static void main method.
Inside main, print: Hello, garden!
Compile the file and run the program.
Change the message, then compile and run it once more.
evidenceChecks: I typed the program rather than pasting it.
I changed the output and saw my new message.
hints: Java file names and public class names need to match exactly, including capital letters.
The output line begins with System.out.println and the message belongs inside quotation marks.
Compile with javac HelloGarden.java, then run with java HelloGarden.
If an error points to a line, first check spelling, quotation marks, parentheses, braces, and semicolons.

questions.prompt: Which command compiles HelloGarden.java into Java bytecode?
questions.correctExplanation: Correct. javac is the Java compiler; it turns the source file into a .class file.
questions.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. javac compiles the .java source file. The java command runs a compiled class.

mascotMessage: Typing it yourself helps your hands learn the shape of Java.

title: Choose a Weather Path
description: Change values and conditions to make a program choose between two messages.
instructions: Create a double variable named temperature and give it a value.
Use if and else to print Warm path when temperature is at least 20.0, otherwise print Cosy path.
Run the program once with a value below 20.0 and once with a value above it.
Try exactly 20.0 and predict the message before running.
evidenceChecks: I tested both branches of the condition.
I predicted what would happen at exactly 20.0.
hints: A condition is a question whose answer is true or false.
The comparison for “at least” is written >=.
The if branch uses braces, followed by else and another pair of braces.
If 20.0 should take the warm path, make sure the equality part of >= is present.

questions.prompt: Which expression is true when temperature is exactly 20.0 or higher?
questions.correctExplanation: Correct. >= includes the boundary value 20.0 as well as larger values.
questions.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. “At least” includes equality, so the comparison needs >=.

mascotMessage: Testing the edge value is how careful programmers learn what a condition really says.

title: Trace the Lily Pads
description: Predict a loop one step at a time before asking Java for the answer.
instructions: On paper, write the values 0, 1, 2, and 3 in a column.
Imagine a loop that starts i at 0, continues while i < 4, and increases i by 1.
Beside each value, write whether i < 4 is true or false.
Write the values you expect the loop to print, then check with a tiny program.
evidenceChecks: I traced the condition before running the code.
I can say why 4 is not printed.
hints: Check the condition before each trip through the loop.
The comparison i < 4 does not include 4.
After printing 3, i becomes 4 and the condition is checked again.
A useful trace table has columns for i, the condition result, and the printed output.

questions.prompt: What does a loop print when it starts with i = 0, continues while i < 4, and prints i before increasing it?
questions.correctExplanation: Correct. The loop prints 0 through 3; when i becomes 4, i < 4 is false.
questions.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The condition is checked before printing, and 4 < 4 is false.

mascotMessage: A pencil trace can make a fast loop slow enough to see.

title: Build a Gentle Countdown
description: Write a loop, then change its direction and stopping point.
instructions: Write a for loop that prints the integers 1 through 5.
Change it so it prints 5 down to 1.
Add Garden ready! after the loop.
Before running, identify the start, condition, and update parts.
evidenceChecks: My countdown prints each intended number once.
I can point to the loop’s start, condition, and update.
hints: A for loop keeps its start, continuation condition, and update inside the parentheses.
For a countdown, start at 5 and subtract 1 after each round.
The countdown should continue while the value is greater than or equal to 1.
If it never stops, check whether the update moves the value toward making the condition false.
mascotMessage: Loops feel safer when you can name their three moving parts.

title: Name a Reusable Idea
description: Create a method that turns a temperature into a short description.
instructions: Write a static method named weatherNote that receives one double value.
Make it return Warm when the value is at least 20.0 and Cosy otherwise.
Call the method from main with three different values and print each result.
Add one call using exactly 20.0.
evidenceChecks: My method uses its parameter rather than a fixed value.
My method returns a String for both possible paths.
I called the method with more than one value.
hints: A method header needs a return type, a name, and a parameter list.
The return type is String and the parameter can be double temperature.
Both the if and else paths need to return a value.
Start with: static String weatherNote(double temperature) { … }
mascotMessage: Giving an idea a good method name is a small act of kindness for future you.

title: Teach Tintinsito When a Loop Stops
description: Explain a loop in plain language and uncover any fuzzy parts.
instructions: Choose one loop you wrote recently.
Explain to Tintinsito what is true before the first iteration.
Explain what changes during one iteration.
Finish this sentence: The loop stops because…
Name one change that could accidentally make the loop continue forever.
evidenceChecks: I explained the stopping condition without reading a definition.
I named a possible infinite-loop mistake.
hints: Plain language is the goal; you do not need special terminology.
Ask which variable changes and which comparison eventually becomes false.
If the important variable never changes, the condition may stay true forever.
Try drawing one arrow from the update back to the condition.
mascotMessage: If you can explain where a loop stops, you are no longer just following its shape.

title: Meet the Array Family
description: Store several values together and visit them safely by index.
instructions: Create an int array containing 6, 7, 4, and 3.
Print the first and last values using their indices.
Use an enhanced for loop to print every value.
Use a normal for loop with the array length to print every value again.
Predict what would happen if you tried to read index 4, but do not add that line to your final program.
evidenceChecks: I know the first and last valid indices for this array.
Both loop versions print all four values.
hints: An array with four items has a length of 4, but its first index is 0.
The last valid index is always length - 1.
A safe indexed loop usually continues while i < values.length.
Trying index 4 in this four-item array causes an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

questions.prompt: An array has length 4. What is its last valid index?

options.text: It depends on the stored values

questions.correctExplanation: Correct. Indexing begins at 0, so the last valid index is length - 1, which is 3.
questions.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. Four items use indices 0, 1, 2, and 3. The last index is length - 1.

mascotMessage: Array positions begin at zero; the length still tells you how many values there are.

title: Find the Tallest Sunflower
description: Write a small method that searches an array for its largest value.
instructions: Write a static method named findLargest that receives an int array and returns an int.
Start with the first array value as the largest value seen so far.
Visit the remaining values and replace the saved value whenever you find a larger one.
Test with {6, 7, 4, 3}, {-8, -2, -11}, and a one-item array.
Explain why starting with 0 would give a wrong answer for some arrays.
evidenceChecks: My method returns 7, -2, and the one item for the three tests.
I used the array data rather than 0 as the initial largest value.
I can explain how the loop maintains the largest value seen so far.
hints: Solve only one piece at a time: method header, initial value, loop, comparison, return.
The first array item is a safer initial answer than 0 because all values might be negative.
The loop can begin at index 1 because index 0 is already stored as the current largest.
Partial shape: int largest = values[0]; then loop from 1, compare values[i] with largest, and return largest.
mascotMessage: A challenge task is a place to notice what you know—not a verdict on you.
